executive_thesis:
Across his mature commentaries on Aristotle's *Physics* and *De Caelo* (c. 1268–1273), Thomas Aquinas articulates a unified ontology and noetics of continuous quantity that bridges natural philosophy and pure geometry without collapsing either into Platonic separatism or empiricist atomism. The cornerstone of this synthesis is laid down in *In II Physicorum*, lectio 3: because dimensive quantity inheres in corporeal substance prior in the order of nature to sensible qualities and physical motion, the intellect can grasp points, lines, surfaces, and solids together with their *per se* attributes while leaving sensible matter out of consideration. Consequently, *there is no falsehood in those who abstract* (*abstrahentium non est mendacium*): the geometer does not judge that lines exist apart from physical bodies, but considers in isolation what is intelligibly prior to heat, weight, and resistance, retaining *intelligible matter*—the homogeneous three-dimensional extension that individuates congruent figures—while leaving behind *sensible matter* (unlike physical definitions, which resemble *the snub* in enclosing a determinate sensible subject, whereas mathematical definitions resemble *the concave* or *curved*). Conversely, the *sciences intermediate between mathematics and physics*—optics, harmonics, and astronomy—descend from pure mathematical demonstrations back to sensible matter, demonstrating physical conclusions through formal quantitative middle terms.

This abstractive hierarchy rests on the deeper categorial and topological architecture developed in *Physics* III, IV, and VI. In *In III Physicorum*, lectio 5, resolving how a single continuous motion realizes both action (*as from the agent*) and passion (*as in the patient*), Aquinas derives all ten Aristotelian categories from *modes of predicating* proportional to *modes of being* (*modi essendi*): substance predicates essence; quantity and quality predicate intrinsic accidents following matter and form respectively (with figure founded as a quality upon quantitative boundaries); relation predicates an intrinsic respect toward another; and the remaining six categories arise by extrinsic denomination from efficient causality (action and passion), extrinsic cosmic measures (*when* from time, *where* and *position* from place), and human rational equipment (*having*). Within this framework, *In IV Physicorum*, lectio 7 demonstrates how *immobile place* becomes known through local translation—the succession of bodies within an invariant containing boundary—and adopts Themistius's solution for the outermost celestial sphere: a rotating homogeneous continuum requires no external container as a whole because its intrinsic parts, consecutive to one another around the circle, exist in place *in potency*. Crucially, as *In VI Physicorum*, lectio 1 proves with geometric rigor, no *continuum*—neither magnitude, motion, nor time—can ever be composed of or resolved into *indivisibles*. Because partless points have no extremes distinct from a remainder, two points can be neither *continuous* (sharing one common extreme), nor *contiguous* (having distinct extremes together without coinciding in position), nor *consecutive* (since a divisible line always intervenes between any two distinct points); points exist strictly as indivisible boundaries, cuts, and intersections of prior continua.

Finally, in *In De Caelo* I, lectio 2 and II, lectio 2, Aquinas integrates the topological completeness of three-dimensional extension with the constructive imagination of classical geometry. Body is the sole *perfect* magnitude because three mutually orthogonal dimensions exhaust divisibility *every way* (*omniquaque*), uniting the formal definition of the continuum (parts joined at a common boundary) with its material definition (divisible into things always further divisible). When geometers state that a moving point generates a line, a moving line a surface, and a moving surface a solid, Aquinas explains that they employ an imaginative and genetic *mode of speaking* (*modus loquendi geometrarum*) that traces dimensional priority by defect from the complete three-dimensional solid rather than positing physical locomotion of partless atoms. Likewise, *In II De Caelo*, lectio 2 distinguishes intrinsic biological and dynamical orientations (*above* and *below*, *before* and *behind*, *right* and *left*) from positional directions in inanimate bodies and mathematical figures, which hold no absolute internal principle of motion and acquire directional orientation solely by relational position (*positio* / *situs*) relative to a chosen frame or observer—anticipating the invariance of Euclidean figures under rigid translation, rotation, and reflection.

conceptual_table.english_term: there is no falsehood in those who abstract
conceptual_table.significance: Epistemological principle guaranteeing the exact truth of geometry: considering dimensive quantity without sensible qualities commits no error because the geometer abstracts by non-consideration rather than asserting separate existence.

Ontological ground of mathematical abstraction: quantity precedes sensible qualities in substance, allowing the intellect to abstract geometric magnitudes from sensible matter while retaining substance under pure extension as intelligible matter.

conceptual_table.english_term: the snub / the concave or curved
conceptual_table.significance: Paradigmatic contrast of definitions: natural definitions resemble *the snub* by including a sensible subject (a nose) in their essence, whereas mathematical definitions resemble *the curved* by prescinding from every sensible subject.

conceptual_table.english_term: sciences intermediate between mathematics and physics
conceptual_table.significance: Disciplines such as optics, harmonics, and astronomy that apply abstract geometric and arithmetic demonstrations to sensible matter, remaining formally mathematical in their middle terms yet terminally natural in their subject.

conceptual_table.english_term: modes of being / modes of predicating
conceptual_table.significance: Architectonic principle of Aquinas's derivation of the ten categories: being is divided analogically rather than univocally because the fundamental ways predicates are affirmed of a subject mirror the ways reality inheres in or denominates substance.

conceptual_table.latin_term: actio ut ab hoc / passio ut in hoc
conceptual_table.english_term: action as from this / passion as in this
conceptual_table.significance: Resolution of the unity of motion with the duality of causal categories: numerically one continuous motion in the mobile is denominated *action* as proceeding from the agent and *passion* as received in the patient.

The innermost immobile boundary of the containing body, first revealed to the intellect through local translation when distinct bodies successively occupy the same surrounding limit without interpenetrating dimensions.

conceptual_table.latin_term: in loco per partes in potentia
conceptual_table.english_term: in place through parts in potency
conceptual_table.significance: Themistius's solution, endorsed by Aquinas against Averroes and Avicenna, explaining rotational motion of an uncontained continuous sphere: while the whole does not change place in subject, its potentially divisible parts succeed one another circularly.

Topological triad governing spatial and temporal order: *continuous* things share one common extreme, *contiguous* things have distinct extremes together, and *consecutive* things have nothing of the same genus intervening between them.

Partless boundaries—such as points on a line or *nows* in time—that possess position or order as extremes of division, but can never touch, overlap partially, or be summed to compose an extended continuum.

Definition of three-dimensional body as the complete and perfect genus of magnitude, exhausting all mutually perpendicular directions of continuous extension so that no transition into a fourth spatial genus occurs.

conceptual_table.english_term: a moving point makes a line
conceptual_table.locus: De Caelo I, lect. 2; II, lect. 2
conceptual_table.significance: The kinematic *mode of speaking* of geometers (*modus loquendi geometrarum*), whereby constructive imagination traces higher-dimensional magnitudes from lower-dimensional boundaries to express generative priority without physical atomism.

The six directional poles (*above* and *below*, *before* and *behind*, *right* and *left*), which belong intrinsically only to animate self-movers and apply to inanimate bodies and geometric figures purely by relational orientation (*quoad nos*).

section_summaries.heading: Physics Book II, Lecture 3 — How the Mathematician Differs from the Natural Philosopher and Why There Is No Falsehood in Those Who Abstract
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Aquinas examines how mathematics and natural philosophy can treat the very same geometric realities—points, lines, surfaces, and solid bodies—without collapsing into a single science. Beginning with two aporiae (that natural bodies possess surfaces, solidities, lengths, and points, and that astronomy simultaneously belongs to mathematics and demonstrates the shapes of natural celestial bodies), Aquinas resolves the difficulty through the distinction of formal perspectives (*rationes considerandi*). Whereas the physicist investigates surfaces, lines, and points precisely insofar as they are boundaries of a mobile natural body endowed with sensible qualities, the mathematician considers them apart from motion and sensible matter. Grounding this epistemic capacity in the ontological order of accidents inhering in substance, Aquinas shows that dimensive quantity accrues to corporeal substance prior to sensible qualities (such as hot, cold, white, or heavy) and the motions rooted in them. Because what is prior in nature does not include what is posterior in its intelligible definition, the intellect can understand quantity and figure with *intelligible matter* (substance as subject to pure extension) while leaving *sensible matter* out of consideration—confirming that *there is no falsehood in those who abstract*, since non-consideration of sensible qualities is not a false judgment of ontological separation.

From this principle Aquinas diagnoses Plato's twofold error—reifying both mathematicals and natural species into separate Ideas by confusing intellectual abstraction with separate existence—and confirms his solution through two decisive signs. First, natural definitions always resemble *the snub* (*simum*), which includes a determinate sensible subject (the nose) in its essence, whereas mathematical definitions—even and odd, straight and *curved* (*curvum*), number, line, and figure—prescind from any sensible subject. Second, the *sciences intermediate between mathematics and physics* (optics, harmonics, and astronomy) invert pure mathematical abstraction by applying abstract geometric and arithmetic theorems back to visual rays, audible sounds, and celestial spheres. Because a science takes its denomination from its terminus, these intermediate sciences are more natural than mathematical, explaining why both the physicist and the astronomer prove that the earth is spherical, yet through distinct middle terms: the physicist from the symmetric downward tendency of heavy parts toward the center, and the astronomer from the curved shadow cast in lunar eclipses and the shifting horizon of visible stars.
key_theses: Mathematics and physics investigate the same extended realities (points, lines, surfaces, and bodies) under distinct formal perspectives: physics treats them as boundaries of mobile natural bodies, whereas mathematics abstracts them from motion and sensible matter.

Dimensive quantity inheres in substance prior to sensible qualities and physical motions; therefore quantity encloses intelligible matter (substance subject to extension) in its notion without enclosing sensible matter.

There is no falsehood in those who abstract (*abstrahentium non est mendacium*), because considering geometric magnitude apart from sensible qualities does not assert that mathematical objects subsist outside sensible bodies, as Plato mistakenly supposed.

Natural definitions follow the model of *the snub* by incorporating sensible matter (flesh and bone, though not individual flesh and bone), whereas mathematical definitions follow the model of *the curved* by excluding sensible matter entirely.

Sciences intermediate between mathematics and physics (optics, harmonics, astronomy) apply pure geometric and arithmetic principles to sensible matter, sharing conclusions with physics while demonstrating them through formal quantitative middle terms.

section_summaries.heading: Physics Book III, Lecture 5 — On Action and Passion and the Division of Being into Ten Categories Proportional to Modes of Predicating
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Commenting on Aristotle's dialectical investigation into where motion resides relative to mover and moved, Aquinas demonstrates that *action* (the act of the active principle) and *passion* (the act of the passive principle) are numerically one and the same continuous motion residing in the mobile subject, yet formally distinct in intelligible definition (*ratio*). If action and passion were two distinct motions, either motion would reside in the unmoved mover or a single mobile would undergo two simultaneous motions toward the very same specific terminus—both of which are impossible. Conversely, identifying action and passion in subject does not entail that teaching is identical in definition with learning or that every agent undergoes change: just as the road from Thebes to Athens and the road from Athens to Thebes, or an abstract spatial interval taken between opposite endpoints, is one in reality (*secundum rem*) yet two in directed notion (*secundum rationem*), so the single continuous motion is *action* insofar as it proceeds *from* the agent (*ut ab hoc*) and *passion* insofar as it is received *in* the patient (*ut in hoc*).

To answer how a merely conceptual distinction within one motion can ground two distinct categories of real being—and how motion can simultaneously belong to quantity, quality, and *where*—Aquinas unfolds his celebrated systematic derivation of the ten Aristotelian categories. Being is not divided univocally like a genus into species, but analogically according to diverse *modes of being* (*modi essendi*), which are strictly proportional to *modes of predicating* (*modi praedicandi*). Predicating what pertains to the essence yields *substance*; predicating what inheres intrinsically yields *quantity* (on the part of matter, furnishing intrinsic length, breadth, and depth), *quality* (on the part of form, including geometric *figure* founded upon lines and surfaces), or *relation* (an intrinsic respect toward another). Finally, predicating by extrinsic denomination yields *action* and *passion* (from external efficient causality), *when* (from time as extrinsic measure), *where* and *position* (from place and the order of parts in place), and *having* (from external instruments fashioned by human reason). Materially considered as an imperfect act in nature, motion reduces to the category of its terminus (quantity, quality, or *where*); formally apprehended as a medium between potency and act implying cause and effect, it grounds the categories of action and passion.
key_theses: Action and passion are numerically one continuous motion residing in the mobile patient, distinguished formally as act proceeding *from* the agent (*ut ab hoc*) versus act received *in* the patient (*ut in hoc*), analogous to one spatial interval traversed in opposite directions.

Being is divided into the ten categories not univocally, like a genus into species, but analogically according to diverse *modes of being* (*modi essendi*) that are proportional to *modes of predicating* (*modi praedicandi*).

Intrinsic inherence generates the categories of quantity (consequent upon matter and providing intrinsic dimensional measure), quality (consequent upon form, with figure founded upon quantitative lines and surfaces), and relation.

Extrinsic denomination by cause and measure generates action and passion (from efficient causality), *when* (from temporal measure), *where* and *position* (*situs*, adding the order of parts in place), and *having* (*habitus*).

Motion as an inchoate reality in nature reduces to the category of its terminus (quantity, quality, or *where*), whereas as a transition from potency to act apprehended between two terms it grounds the categories of action and passion.

section_summaries.heading: Physics Book IV, Lecture 7 — On the Definition of Immobile Place from Local Translation and Themistius's Solution
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Having established Aristotle's definition of *immobile place* as the innermost immobile surface of the containing body, Aquinas confronts the classic cosmological and topological aporia of the outermost celestial sphere: since nothing exists outside the universe to contain it, how can the outermost sphere be in place, given that it manifestly rotates locally? Aquinas first rejects the hypothesis of self-subsistent three-dimensional void space interpenetrating corporeal dimensions as ontologically impossible. He then subjects four historical Peripatetic and Arabic solutions to rigorous critique: Alexander of Aphrodisias's denial that the outermost sphere moves in place at all; Avicenna's claim that it moves in the category of *position* (*situs*) rather than *where* (refuted because every species of *position* consists in an indivisible configuration admitting no *per se* continuous succession, and moreover presupposes *place*); Avempace's proposal that a circularly moving body is located by the convex surface of the inner sphere around which it revolves (violating the axioms that place contains and equals the located); and Averroes's contention that the outermost sphere is in place *per accidens* through the fixity of its central body (rejected as incongruous because the center is wholly extrinsic to the substance of the outer shell).

Aquinas decisively endorses the solution of Themistius, grounding it in the epistemological origin of the concept of place itself: place would never be sought save on account of local motion (translation), which reveals place through the succession of distinct bodies within one identical spatial bound. Whereas rectilinear translation requires one whole body to vacate a place and another whole body to enter it—demanding an external containing place *per se* for the whole—circular rotation preserves the whole body within the selfsame spatial region in subject while its parts continuously replace one another in subject around the circumference. Although the parts of a homogeneous *continuum* (illustrated by water rotating within a vessel) are not actually divided like a heap of *contiguous* stones, they are divisible and *consecutive* to one another around the circle, mutually containing and contained *in potency*. Thus the outermost sphere is in place *per accidens* by reason of its intrinsic parts existing potentially in place—a minimal, uniform mode of local variation uniquely suited to the first cosmic motion.
key_theses: The existence and nature of place become known through local translation—the observed succession of distinct bodies occupying the same containing boundary—while self-subsistent three-dimensional space interpenetrating bodies is impossible.

Avicenna's theory of *per se* motion in the category of *position* (*situs*) fails because each species of *situs* consists in an indivisible order of parts that admits no continuous succession of more and less apart from local motion.

Averroes's claim that the outermost sphere is in place *per accidens* through the immobility of an extrinsic center violates Aristotle's definition of *per accidens* location, which requires inherence or containment within what is located.
Following Themistius, circular motion does not require the whole rotating continuum to change place in subject, but only its parts to succeed one another continuously in the same spatial positions.

Unlike a heap of separated, *contiguous* stones whose parts are in place in act, a homogeneous circular *continuum* has parts that are *consecutive* and mutually containing in potency, placing the whole in place *per accidens* through its intrinsic parts.

section_summaries.heading: Physics Book VI, Lecture 1 — That No Continuum (Line, Time, or Motion) Can Be Composed of Indivisible Points
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Opening Book VI on the quantitative divisibility of motion, Aquinas presents Aristotle's apodictic demonstration that no *continuum*—whether a geometric line, temporal duration, or continuous motion—can be composed out of *indivisibles* (such as points or *nows*). Resuming the topological definitions established in Book V—that *continuous* things are those whose extremes are one, *contiguous* things (things in contact) are those whose extremes are together, and *consecutive* things are those with nothing of their own genus intervening between them—Aquinas systematically eliminates every conceivable mode in which partless points could form a line. First, points cannot be *continuous* or *contiguous* by their extremes, because an extreme (*ultimum*) implies a distinction between boundary and bounded part, whereas a partless indivisible admits no internal diversity of parts. Second, if two indivisibles touched at all, neither part-to-part nor part-to-whole contact would be possible; whole would have to touch whole, causing the two points to coincide completely in site (*situs*) rather than generating distinct spatial positions capable of extending a magnitude. Third, points cannot stand *consecutively* to one another, because between any two positionally distinct points an extended line always intervenes (and between any two *nows*, an interval of time).

Aquinas reinforces this topological proof with a second principal demonstration from the Book III definition of the continuum as that which is infinitely divisible: since anything is divisible into the elements out of which it is composed, a continuum composed of indivisibles would divide into partless atoms, destroying infinite divisibility. Finally, Aquinas closes every loophole by proving the two supporting lemmas rigorously: any medium separating two non-touching, positionally distinct points cannot be an indivisible (on pain of an infinite regress of intervening gaps) nor a divisible composed of indivisibles, and must therefore be a *continuum* divisible into things always further divisible—namely, a line; conversely, no continuum can ever be resolved into indivisibles without requiring partless indivisibles to touch one another.
key_theses: From the Book V definitions of *continuous* (extremes are one), *contiguous* (extremes are together), and *consecutive* (nothing of the same genus between), it follows apodictically that no continuum is composed of *indivisibles*.
Indivisible points possess no internal distinction between boundary (*ultimum*) and remainder, and therefore can neither share a common extreme nor place distinct extremes together.
If two partless points touched, whole would touch whole, collapsing them into a single spatial position rather than producing the positionally distinct parts required for an extended continuum.

No two points on a line (nor two *nows* in time) can be *consecutive*, because between any two positionally distinct points there necessarily intervenes a continuous, infinitely divisible line segment.

Every continuum is divisible solely into things always further divisible (*in semper divisibilia*), never into partless atoms; points exist as indivisible boundaries and cuts of continua, not as constituent building blocks.

section_summaries.heading: On the Heavens Book I, Lecture 2 — On the Perfection of Three-Dimensional Body and the Geometers' Mode of Speaking of a Moving Point
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Launching the treatise on the corporeal universe, Aquinas synthesizes Aristotle's dual definitions of the *continuum*—the formal logical definition of the *Categories* (that whose parts are joined at one common boundary) and the material physical definition of *Physics* and *De Caelo* (that which is divisible into things always further divisible)—in order to define *body* as a continuum divisible *every way* (*omniquaque*), that is, across all three dimensions. Dividing continuous magnitude into line (divisible in one direction), plane or surface (divisible in two), and body (divisible in three), Aquinas analyzes Aristotle's appeal to Pythagorean ternary symbolism, liturgical custom, and universal linguistic usage (where *both* is said of two, and *all* first of three) to show that three carries the formal ratio of totality (*beginning*, *middle*, and *end*). Following Simplicius, Aquinas makes a crucial methodological observation: Aristotle offers these ternary signs as probable confirmations suited to natural philosophy while presupposing the strict geometric demonstration from mathematics—exemplified by Ptolemy's proof that no more than three mutually perpendicular lines can meet at one and the same point.

Because *all*, *whole*, and *perfect* share the same formal notion of completeness, three-dimensional body alone is the *perfect* magnitude, possessing every mode of continuity. From this completeness Aquinas explains a fundamental asymmetry in dimensional generation: whereas geometers imaginatively describe a transition from point to line, from line to surface, and from surface to solid—employing the *mode of speaking* of geometers (*modus loquendi geometrarum*) who imagine that a moving point makes a line, a moving line makes a surface, and a moving surface makes a body—no analogous transition can pass from body into a fourth genus of magnitude. Every such dimensional progression arises from a dimensional defect in the lower boundary (just as motion belongs to the imperfect), whereas three-dimensional body exhibits no dimensional lack. Finally, while particular bodies are three-dimensionally complete yet externally bounded by *contiguous* neighbors (making them imperfect and *many*), the total corporeal universe is perfect *every way*, comprehending both all three dimensions and all bodies.
key_theses: Aristotle's formal definition of the *continuum* (parts joined at one common boundary) and material definition (divisible into things always further divisible) converge in defining body as a continuum divisible *every way* (*omniquaque*).

While Aristotle adduces Pythagorean ternary arguments and common speech as probable signs in natural science, strict demonstration that spatial dimensions are exactly three belongs to mathematics—as in Ptolemy's proof that at most three mutually perpendicular lines can meet at one point.

Because *all*, *whole*, and *perfect* signify formal integrity, three-dimensional body is the sole complete magnitude, whereas line (one-dimensional) and surface (two-dimensional) are dimensionally incomplete boundaries.

When geometers say that a moving point makes a line, a moving line a surface, and a moving surface a body, they employ an imaginative constructive *mode of speaking* reflecting dimensional defect, which terminates irreversibly at three-dimensional body.

Particular bodies are dimensionally complete in genus yet limited by contact with exterior bodies, whereas the universe as a whole is *omniquaque* perfect both in three-dimensionality and in comprehending all bodies.

section_summaries.heading: On the Heavens Book II, Lecture 2 — On Positional Directions in Natural Bodies and How They Are Considered by Position in Mathematical Figures
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Investigating whether positional polarities such as *right* and *left* belong intrinsically to the celestial sphere as the Pythagoreans claimed, Aquinas develops a rigorous ontology of directional orientation (*differentiae positionum*) across animate organisms, inanimate physical bodies, and abstract geometric figures. Drawing on *On the Progression of Animals*, Aquinas establishes that the three directional oppositions—*above* and *below* (governing length), *right* and *left* (governing breadth), and *before* and *behind* (governing depth)—belong *per se* and intrinsically only to living self-movers endowed with determinate organic parts from which vital motions originate: plants possess only *above* and *below* (with the root functioning organically as *above* by drawing nourishment), sessile animals add *before* and *behind* through sense perception, and locally mobile perfect animals possess all six directions. Furthermore, these three axes stand in a strict hierarchy both dimensionally (length precedes breadth and breadth precedes depth, just as line precedes surface and surface precedes body—since according to geometers a moving line generates a surface) and dynamically (*above* is the primary origin of growth and sensory command, *before* is the goal of sensory orientation, and *right* is the starting limb of locomotion).

By contrast, inanimate bodies and artificial or mathematical objects possess no intrinsic active principle of motion in one determinate part rather than another: heavy and light elements move uniformly from every side toward their natural center or periphery, while artificial and geometric figures lack internal self-motion altogether. Consequently, directional terms (*above* and *below*, *right* and *left*, *before* and *behind*) are predicated of inanimate things and geometric figures solely *by comparison to us* (*per comparationem ad nos*) in three relational modes: by direct alignment with our own sides (as in augury), by anthropomorphic likeness (as in a statue), or by mirror-image inversion (*contraria positio*, as in a specular reflection, where right opposes our left). This relational relativity is proved by rotational invariance: turning an inanimate object or geometric figure reverses its *right* and *left* relative to us, whereas an organism retains its intrinsic right and left under every rotation. Aquinas concludes by refuting the Pythagorean table of ten opposites for attributing *right* and *left* universally to all things while omitting the prior axes of *above* and *below* as well as *before* and *behind*.
key_theses: The six directional differences (*above* and *below*, *before* and *behind*, *right* and *left*) belong intrinsically and *per se* only to animate bodies possessing internal principles of nutrition, sensation, and locomotion in determinate organs.

Dimensionally and genetically, *above* (principle of length) is prior to *right* (principle of breadth), and *right* is prior to *before* (principle of depth), mirroring the geometric priority of line to surface (where a moving line generates a surface) and surface to solid.

Inanimate bodies, artifacts, and mathematical figures possess no intrinsic directional polarity, because they lack determinate parts initiating self-motion; when rotated, their apparent *right* and *left* invert.

Positional directions are attributed to inanimate and geometric objects solely *by comparison to us* (*quoad nos*) in three ways: direct observer alignment, anthropomorphic correspondence (as in statues), and mirror-image inversion (*in speculo*).

The Pythagoreans erred both in projecting *right* and *left* onto all things via their moral table of ten opposites and in attributing *right* and *left* to the cosmos while neglecting the dimensionally and causally prior principle of *above* and *below*.

section_notes.heading: Physics Book II, Lecture 3 — How the Mathematician Differs from the Natural Philosopher and Why There Is No Falsehood in Those Who Abstract
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas's exposition comments on Aristotle's *Physics* II.2 (193b22–194a12), the locus classicus distinguishing natural philosophy (*physike*) from mathematics against Platonic Realism. Where Aristotle tersely remarks that the mathematician separates (*chorizei*) surfaces, volumes, lengths, and points in thought from motion without generating falsehood (*oude ginetai pseudos chorizonton*, 193b35—rendered in the Moerbeke-vetus tradition as *neque fit mendacium abstrahentium*), Aquinas supplies a full metaphysical justification drawn from *Metaphysics* VII.10–11 (1036a9–12) and Averroes's *Long Commentary on the Physics* (II, comm. 18–20). By establishing the ontological order in which accidents accrue to corporeal substance—dimensive quantity first, then sensible qualities, then active and passive powers and local or qualitative motions—Aquinas explains *why* mathematical abstraction is non-deceptive while Platonic separation of natural forms (flesh, bone, man) fails. Likewise, Aquinas's analysis of *the snub* (*to simon*, 194a1–7) versus *the curved* (*to koilon*) and of the *ta physikotera ton mathematon* (194a7–12: optics, harmonics, astronomy) harmonizes Aristotle's *Physics* II.2 with *Posterior Analytics* I.7–13 (75b14–17, 78b34–79a16) on subalternated sciences and *De Caelo* II.14 (297a8–298a20) on the physical versus astronomical proofs of the earth's sphericity, echoing Simplicius (*In Phys.*, ed. Diels, 290–293) who cites Geminus and Posidonius on the methodological boundary between causal physics and saving-the-phenomena mathematical astronomy.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: In Euclid's *Elements*, Book I Definitions 1–7 and Book XI Definitions 1–2 define point, line, straight line, surface, plane surface, and solid without a single reference to weight, temperature, optical medium, or physical resistance. Aquinas's commentary on *Physics* II.3 provides the exact epistemological warrant for Euclid's procedure: the Euclidean line is ontological reality—the very quantitative limit existing in natural bodies—considered apart from sensible matter (*linea naturalis abstracte considerata*). Moreover, Aquinas's distinction between pure geometry and the *sciences intermediate between mathematics and physics* directly illuminates the Euclidean corpus itself, where pure planar and stereometric theorems in the *Elements* are subalternated in Euclid's *Optics* and *Catoptrics* (applying abstract straight lines and equal angles to visual rays, *lineae visuales*) and in the Euclidean *Sectio Canonis* (applying arithmetic ratios of numbers to consonant musical intervals). Even the dual demonstration of terrestrial sphericity in n. 9 illustrates how Euclidean circular and spherical geometry furnishes formal *propter quid* middle terms (lunar shadow cross-sections and angular stellar altitudes) for phenomena grounded physically in elemental gravitation.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae* (Chapter II, § 7, linking *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 85, a. 1, ad 2 directly with *In II Phys.*, lect. 3, n. 5, and Chapter III, § 2), Peter Hoenen S.J. makes Aquinas's ordering of quantity prior to sensible qualities the linchpin of geometric exactitude and necessity. Against John Stuart Mill's empiricist reduction of geometric figures to inexact copies of sense impressions (*minimum visibile*) and J. Wellstein's voluntarist claim that exact boundaries require an arbitrary act of the will, Hoenen argues that intellectual abstraction inspecting the phantasm grasps extended substance purely *as extended*—that is, clothed in *intelligible matter* while prescinding from all sensible qualities. Because *there is no falsehood in those who abstract*, the intellect sees with apodictic certainty that three-dimensional extension *per se* admits exact indivisible boundaries (surfaces, lines, and points) even if microscopic physical surfaces in sensible nature are violently wrinkled. Thus *In II Phys.*, lect. 3 grounds Hoenen's central thesis that mathematical existence is neither a Platonic fiction nor a formalist postulate, but an objective necessity apprehended in real extension.
section_notes.geometor_significance: For the GEOMETOR initiative, Aquinas's principle that *there is no falsehood in those who abstract* defines the philosophical divide between exact symbolic geometry and numerical floating-point approximation. When ``geometor.model`` represents points, lines, and circles through exact algebraic expressions in SymPy—preserving quadratic and higher polynomial surds such as the square root of five rather than truncating coordinates to finite IEEE-754 floats or rasterized pixels—it enacts Aquinas's intellectual abstraction from sensible matter (physical measurement noise and display resolution) while retaining *intelligible matter* (the continuous algebraic plane in which distinct congruent figures are individuated by coordinate position). Equally, Aquinas's account of the *sciences intermediate between mathematics and physics* models the relationship within the GEOMETOR ecosystem between pure symbolic construction in ``geometor.model`` and ``geometor.elements`` on the one hand, and applied structural analysis in ``geometor.phyllotaxis`` or visual SVG rendering in ``geometor.explorer`` on the other, where pure geometric proportions and golden-ratio invariants are re-applied to botanical growth patterns and sensible visual diagrams.

section_notes.heading: Physics Book III, Lecture 5 — On Action and Passion and the Division of Being into Ten Categories Proportional to Modes of Predicating
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *Physics* III.3 (202a13–202b29), Aquinas resolves Aristotle's famous aporia on the locus of motion—whether teaching (*didaxis*) and learning (*mathesis*), or action (*poiesis*) and passion (*pathesis*), are two motions or one—using Aristotle's own topological analogy of a single road between Thebes and Athens (202b13–14) and a single spatial interval between two points (*to metaxy*, 202a18–20). Going far beyond a mere paraphrase, Aquinas inserts in nn. 14–17 one of the two great categorial deductions in his entire corpus (parallel to *In V Metaphysicorum*, lect. 9, n. 890), silently correcting Averroes (*In Phys.* III, comm. 20–23) and Avicenna on whether motion belongs to a category *via ad rem* (*motus ad formam*) or *forma fluens*. By distinguishing what motion is *in rerum natura* (an imperfect act reduced to the category of its terminus: quantity, quality, or *where*) from what reason apprehends in motion as a directed transition from agent to patient (grounding the extrinsic denominations of action and passion), Aquinas preserves both *Categories* 4 (1b25–2a4) and *Physics* V.1–2 (225b5–9) within a single analogical metaphysics of being.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Two profound Euclidean insights emerge within Aquinas's categorial deduction in *In III Phys.*, lect. 5. First, in n. 15 Aquinas explicitly locates geometric *figure* (*figura*) in the fourth species of the category of *quality* (*Categories* 8, 10a11–24), observing that figure follows upon form yet is founded immediately upon dimensive *quantity*—specifically in lines and surfaces as quantitative boundaries (*sicut color in superficie, et figura in lineis vel in superficiebus*). This explains why Euclidean figures possess both metric magnitude (equality of area or length, governed by Common Notions 1–4) and qualitative shape (similarity of rectilinear figures in *Elements* Book VI Def. 1, governed by angular equality and proportional sides independent of scale). Second, Aquinas's analysis in nn. 10–12 of the spatial distance (*spatium distantium*) between two points—identical *in abstracto* as a metric segment *AB* = *BA*, yet distinct *in concreto* when applied to ordered endpoints *from A to B* versus *from B to A*—captures the exact distinction in Euclidean construction between an undirected segment and a directed ray or circle construction (Postulate 3, where one endpoint serves as stationary center and the other determines radial extremity).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Peter Hoenen S.J. explicitly singles out *In III Physicorum*, lect. 5 in the Appendix (§ 5, p. 341) of *De Noetica Geometriae* alongside *In V Metaphysicorum*, lect. 9 as the master text demonstrating how Aquinas constructs the Aristotelian categories from *modes of being* (*modi essendi*) proportional to *modes of predicating* (*modi praedicandi*). For Hoenen, this text proves that human intellectual apprehension does not grasp naked static quiddities alone, but abstracts distinct existential and relational modes—inherence (*esse in*), substantiality (*esse per se*), and fluent actuality (*esse fluens* in motion). Moreover, in Chapter IV (§ 2 and § 4.2), Hoenen builds directly on the Thebes-to-Athens / *hinc illuc* directional analysis of *Phys.* III.3 and IV.11: while a static line segment *AB* is one single extension, actuating motion or passage through its endpoints reveals two really distinct, inverse *directions* (*A* to *B* versus *B* to *A*), showing that directional order (*thesis*) and quantitative measure are complementary intelligible aspects of the geometric continuum.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's analysis of action *as from this* (*ut ab hoc*) and passion *as in this* (*ut in hoc*), together with his placement of *figure* as a form-like quality supervening on quantitative boundaries, resonates directly with constructive geometry as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in ``geometor.model``. Every compass-and-straightedge step in a GEOMETOR construction—joining two parent points to produce a line, or centering a circle at one point through another to cut an existing locus—embodies a single constructive operation that is simultaneously *active* with respect to its ancestral parent elements (*ut ab hoc*) and *receptive* in instantiating derived child intersections (*ut in hoc*). Furthermore, Aquinas's categorial distinction between intrinsic quantitative measure (length, breadth, depth) and qualitative figure grounded on boundaries mirrors the separation between metric coordinate evaluation and projective or proportional invariants studied in ``geometor.divine`` and ``geometor.pappus``, where golden sections and harmonic cross-ratios persist across scale and transformation as qualitative structural forms supervening upon continuous extension.

section_notes.heading: Physics Book IV, Lecture 7 — On the Definition of Immobile Place from Local Translation and Themistius's Solution
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas expounds *Physics* IV.5 (212a31–212b29), where Aristotle applies his definition of place—*the first immobile boundary of what contains* (*to tou periechontos peras akinēton prōton*, 212a20)—to the cosmos as a whole. Because the aporia of the outermost sphere's diurnal rotation became one of the fiercest battlegrounds of ancient and medieval natural philosophy, Aquinas stages in nn. 3–9 a magisterial disputation surveying John Philoponus's and the Stoics' three-dimensional void space (*spatium dimensiones habens*), Alexander of Aphrodisias, Avicenna (*Sufficientia* II.3, positing motion in *situs*), Avempace / Ibn Bajja (locating a sphere by its inner convex core), Averroes (*In Phys.* IV, comm. 43–45, positing *per accidens* location via the immobile earth at the center), and Themistius (*In Phys.* IV, ed. Schenkl, 120–122). Siding decisively with Themistius against Averroes (whom Aquinas even criticizes in n. 15 for forcing Aristotle's text on water), Aquinas shows how Aristotle's distinction between parts existing *potentially* in place within a homogeneous continuum (*homoimeres*) versus *actually* in place within a *contiguous* heap resolves the paradox without surrendering the relational surface-ontology of place.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's critique of self-subsistent void space (n. 3), Avicenna's indivisibility of *situs* (n. 4), Avempace's inner-boundary theory (n. 5), and Themistius's rotational invariance (nn. 7–14) turns throughout on Euclidean geometry. Against Avempace, Aquinas invokes the Euclidean axioms of containment and equality (*Elements* Common Notion 4: things coinciding with one another are equal to one another): the concave inner surface of a hollow shell is strictly smaller in area than its outer volume and fails to bound it externally. Even more strikingly, Aquinas's analysis in n. 7 of a sphere rotating in place—where the whole sphere remains in the selfsame spatial locus *in subject* while its circularly ordered parts continuously exchange positions—corresponds directly to Euclid's genetic definition of the sphere in *Elements* Book XI Definition 14 (the figure comprehended when a semicircle revolves around its fixed diameter until it returns to the same position) and underpins the Euclidean method of superposition (*epharmozein*) in *Elements* I.4, I.8, and III.24, which presupposes that spatial translation and rotation neither stretch nor deform a figure's metric determinations.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae*, Appendix § 2 (*Hoc movetur, ergo locus est*, pp. 115–138), Peter Hoenen S.J. explicitly cites and transcribes *In IV Physicorum*, lect. 7, n. 7 as a 'beautiful text' (*pulchrum textum*) establishing an intuitive existential nexus against Humean and Kantian skepticism: local translation immediately manifests the existence of place through the succession of bodies within an invariant surrounding extension. Moreover, in Chapter IV (§§ 1–3, pp. 61–158), Hoenen connects Aristotle's and Aquinas's doctrine of translation and rotation in *Phys.* IV with the foundation of geometric congruence against Bertrand Russell and Henri Poincaré. Russell objected that moving a triangle in *Elements* I.4 treats spatial points as material particles, while Poincaré claimed geometry depends empirically on physical rigid bodies. Hoenen replies via Aquinas's *materia intelligibilis* and rotational continuity: just as the parts of Themistius's homogeneous sphere continuously succeed one another in congruent positions without physical deformation, pure extension as the principle of geometric individuation guarantees *a priori* that any figure realized in one site can be identically realized across a continuous succession of sites.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's twin doctrines in *In IV Phys.*, lect. 7—that place is not an empty Cartesian pixel-box existing prior to extended bodies, and that circular rotation maps a homogeneous continuum onto itself in subject while permuting its parts—illuminate how ``geometor.model`` conceives spatial reference without arbitrary grid discretization. In ``geometor.model``, the geometric plane is not a pre-allocated finite array of raster cells; rather, a relational coordinate frame is anchored by two initial foundational points that define the unit interval, from which every subsequent locus is generated by straightedge and compass incidence—an exact computational counterpart to Aristotle's principle that local determinations arise only from extended bodies and their mutual boundaries. Likewise, Aquinas's contrast between rectilinear translation (which shifts a whole figure into an extrinsic place) and circular rotation (which cyclically permutes consecutive parts within a self-contained locus) mirrors the interplay of linear extensions and circular compass sweeps in ``geometor.elements`` and ``geometor.explorer``, where rotational symmetry around a center generates invariant regular polygons and golden-angle phyllotactic rings.

section_notes.heading: Physics Book VI, Lecture 1 — That No Continuum (Line, Time, or Motion) Can Be Composed of Indivisible Points
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas comments on the celebrated opening chapter of *Physics* VI (231a21–231b18), where Aristotle launches his refutation of spatial, temporal, and kinematic atomism (directed historically against Democritus, Xenocrates' indivisible lines, and Zeno's paradoxes, and elaborated by Simplicius, *In Phys.* 925–935, Themistius, and Averroes, *In Phys.* VI, comm. 1–6). Importing the three topological relations rigorously defined in *Physics* V.3 (226b18–227a32)—*suneches* (*continuum*, whose extremes are one), *haptomenon* (*contactum* / *contiguum*, whose extremes are together in the same immediate place), and *ephexes* (*consequenter se habens*, between which nothing of the same genus intervenes)—Aquinas constructs a tight syllogistic dilemma reinforced by the Book III.1 (200b18–20) definition of the continuum as infinitely divisible. Every escape route for point-atomism is sealed in nn. 7–8: two distinct points cannot touch (whole-to-whole contact collapses positional distinction), nor be *consecutive* without a gap, and any gap between two points must itself be infinitely divisible into further divisibles (*in semper divisibilia*), establishing strict isomorphism across spatial magnitude, motion, and time.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's commentary on *Physics* VI.1 is the indispensable philosophical key to reading the opening definitions of Euclid's *Elements* Book I without falling into point-set anachronism. Euclid defines a point as *that which has no part* (*semeion estin hou meros outhen*, Def. 1), a line as *breadthless length* (Def. 2), and—crucially—*the extremities of a line are points* (*grammes de perata semeia*, Def. 3), parallel to Book I Def. 6 (*the extremities of a surface are lines*) and Book XI Def. 2 (*the extremity of a solid is a surface*). Far from building lines out of points like beads on a string, Euclid treats the continuous line as ontologically prior to its endpoint markers and internal section points! Furthermore, Aquinas's theorem that every continuum is divisible *in semper divisibilia* directly underwrites *Elements* Book I Proposition 10 (bisecting any given finite straight line), Book X Proposition 1 (the exhaustion principle of endless bisection), Book X Proposition 2 (incommensurable magnitudes whose Euclidean *antenairesis* never terminates in a common atomic unit), and Book II Proposition 11 / Book VI Proposition 30 (cutting a line in extreme and mean ratio, whose golden-section anthyphairesis continues *in infinitum*).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae* (Chapter III, §§ 1–2, pp. 88–178), Peter Hoenen S.J. deploys the Aristotelian-Thomistic continuum doctrine of *Physics* VI.1 to diagnose the foundational crisis of nineteenth- and twentieth-century arithmetized analysis (Cantor, Dedekind, Wellstein, Russell). Modern rigorists sought to build the geometric continuum upward from an uncountable point-set because they mistakenly began with the point as an isolated corpuscle shrunk to zero (*Grenzprozess*), rendering its mathematical existence unintelligible. Reversing that order with Aristotle and Aquinas, Hoenen begins from the primary intellective datum: three-dimensional continuous extension, whose first *propria passio* is infinite divisibility. When an extended magnitude is divided without separating its parts, the boundary *between* the parts—through which transition occurs in an indivisible—emerges in act: first the surface, then the line, and finally the point, an *indivisible having position*. Because points exist in potency within the undivided continuum and arise in act only as indivisible cuts or intersections, no collection of points—finite or transfinite—can ever constitute extension by *contact* or *consecutiveness*; rather, between any two constructible points an infinitely divisible line segment necessarily intervenes.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Nowhere does Aquinas's philosophy of mathematics speak more directly to GEOMETOR than in *In VI Physicorum*, lect. 1. Digital graphics engines approximate geometry on discrete pixel or floating-point lattices—a computational atomism in which lines are literally *consecutive* arrays of indivisible raster points, causing false misses or rounded drift whenever two loci intersect at irrational coordinates. By contrast, ``geometor.model`` implements the exact Thomistic ontology of the continuum: lines and circles are represented as continuous algebraic loci (linear and quadratic polynomial equations), and points arise *solely* as exact symbolic boundaries and intersections (*termini*) where two continuous loci cut one another. Moreover, Aquinas's proof that between any two distinct points lies a continuum divisible *in semper divisibilia* is the exact mathematical condition enabling the golden ratio (*phi*) investigations of ``geometor.divine``: because the golden section is quadratic and irrational, cutting a segment in extreme and mean ratio induces a self-similar cascade of nested golden sections without ever hitting an indivisible atomic quantum.

section_notes.heading: On the Heavens Book I, Lecture 2 — On the Perfection of Three-Dimensional Body and the Geometers' Mode of Speaking of a Moving Point
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on the opening argument of *De Caelo* I.1 (268a1–268b10), Aquinas harmonizes the formal definition of the continuum in *Categories* 6 (5a1–2: parts joined at a common boundary, *pros hena koinon horon*) with the material definition in *Physics* III.1 and VI.1 (*eis aei diaireta diaireton*) to establish corporeal three-dimensionality. Particularly noteworthy is Aquinas's critical methodological restraint in n. 7, drawn directly from Simplicius's *Commentary on De Caelo* (ed. Heiberg, 6–9; translated into Latin by William of Moerbeke in 1271, immediately utilized by Aquinas): recognizing that Aristotle's appeal to Pythagorean triads, religious libations, and linguistic usage (*ambo* vs. *omnes*) is dialectically probable rather than apodictic, Aquinas cites Claudius Ptolemy's lost treatise *On Dimensionality* (*Peri diastaseos*, preserved in Simplicius), which proves geometrically that at most three mutually perpendicular straight lines can intersect at a single point. Equally incisive is n. 9, explaining Aristotle's remark on impossibility of *metabasis eis allo genos* beyond solid body (268b1–5) by identifying the fluxion of point into line, line into surface, and surface into body as an imaginative idiom of geometers (cf. *De Anima* I.4, 409a3–5).
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's synthesis in *In I De Caelo*, lect. 2 bridges the planar geometry of *Elements* Books I–VI and the solid stereometry of Books XI–XIII. Ptolemy's three-perpendiculars proof cited by Aquinas in n. 7 rests directly on *Elements* Book XI Propositions 4–6 and Definition 3–4 (a straight line perpendicular to a plane is at right angles to all straight lines meeting it in that plane; and through a given point on a plane only one perpendicular straight line can be erected, exhausting orthogonal dimensionality at three). Simultaneously, Aquinas's careful gloss on the *modus loquendi geometrarum*—that a moving point makes a line, a moving line a surface, and a moving surface a solid—illuminates both the classical Greek tradition reported by Proclus (*In Eucl.* 97.6–13) and Heron of Alexandria, and Euclid's own kinematic definitions of the sphere, cone, and cylinder in *Elements* Book XI Definitions 14, 18, and 21 (generated by rotating a semicircle, right triangle, and rectangle around a fixed axis), clarifying that constructive generation expresses dimensional dependency without violating the non-atomistic continuum of *Physics* VI.1.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: Peter Hoenen S.J. cites *In I De Caelo*, lect. 2, n. 9 verbatim in *De Noetica Geometriae* (Chapter IV, § 2, p. 128 and fn. 9, paired with *In II De Caelo*, lect. 2, n. 11 and *In IV Phys.*, lect. 18, n. 4) when evaluating kinematic descriptions in pure geometry. Hoenen shows that Aquinas strikes the exact balance between static ontological rigor and dynamic constructive fruitfulness: strictly speaking, a line cannot be *defined* quidditatively through a moving point without circularity (since motion already presupposes an extended path along which the point moves, as Hoenen demonstrated in Chapter III, § 1), which is why Aquinas attributes this idiom to the *imagination* of geometers (*imaginantes quod punctus motus facit lineam*). Yet as a genetic *description* for tracing special curves (such as Archimedes' spiral or Hippias's quadratrix, where time enters as an auxiliary parameter and is subsequently eliminated to leave a pure geometric locus), kinematic imagination is completely legitimate because it rests on the intelligible continuity and directionality of three-dimensional extension—and in Chapter III, § 2.3, Hoenen likewise echoes Aquinas and Ptolemy on the intuitive clarity of three dimensions against uncritical four-dimensional spatial speculation.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's dual insight in *In I De Caelo*, lect. 2—the completeness of three-dimensional orthogonal extension and the distinction between ontological continuum structure and the constructive *mode of speaking* of geometers—maps directly onto the architecture of GEOMETOR. In ``geometor.explorer`` and ``geometor.model``, constructions unfold sequentially in time as animated sweeps of straightedges and compasses across the canvas, appealing to the geometer's constructive imagination (*modus loquendi geometrarum*) to reveal how complex harmonic configurations emerge step by step from simple seeds. Yet beneath that kinematic animation lies the timeless algebraic continuum of SymPy equations, in which every locus exists complete in its formal definition rather than being assembled out of discrete motion-steps. Furthermore, the culmination of three-dimensional completeness studied in *De Caelo* I.2 points directly toward ``geometor.pacioli`` and *Elements* Book XIII, where planar golden-ratio sections ascend into the five regular Platonic solids—above all the dodecahedron and icosahedron—inscribed within the complete three-dimensional sphere.

section_notes.heading: On the Heavens Book II, Lecture 2 — On Positional Directions in Natural Bodies and How They Are Considered by Position in Mathematical Figures
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas comments here on the first half of *De Caelo* II.2 (284b6–285b8), where Aristotle critiques the Pythagorean attribution of *right* and *left* to the cosmos (cf. *Metaphysics* I.5, 986a22–26, the ten-column *systoichia* of principles) by importing the biological mechanics of *De Incessu Animalium* (*On the Progression of Animals*, chs. 2–5, 704b12–706b16) and *De Anima* II.4 / III.9–10. Following Simplicius (*In De Caelo*, ed. Heiberg, 383–393), Aquinas distinguishes three senses of dimensional priority—by dimensional magnitude (length, breadth, depth), by genetic construction (line, surface, body), and by causal origin of vital motion (nutritive *above*, sensory *before*, locomotive *right*)—and highlights the pivotal philosophical contrast in nn. 6–7 (285a1–10): whereas organisms possess intrinsic functional chirality and polarity independent of external orientation, inanimate bodies and geometric objects lack internal directional principles and receive *above* and *below*, *right* and *left*, and *before* and *behind* solely *quoad nos*—including enantiomorphic inversion in specular reflection (*in speculo*).
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: In Aristotle's Greek text at *De Caelo* II.2, 285a1–4 (reflected in Aquinas's analysis of objects lacking an intrinsic principle of motion in nn. 6–7 and geometric generation in n. 11), triangles and squares are the classic exemplars of inanimate/mathematical objects whose *above*, *below*, *right*, and *left* are assigned purely by positional convention (*thesei* / *per comparationem ad nos*) and reverse whenever the figure is rotated. This principle is fundamental to Euclid's *Elements*: in Book I Definitions 20–22 and Propositions 4, 8, and 26, a triangle's 'base' (*basis*), 'vertex' (*koruphe*), 'left side,' and 'right side' are never intrinsic properties of the figure itself, as Euclid explicitly signals in I.4 and I.5 by choosing whichever side serves the proof as base. Even more remarkably, Aquinas's third relational mode in n. 7—*contraria positio* in a mirror image (*imago quae resultat in speculo*), where right and left interchange while preserving figure (*conveniunt in figura*, n. 9)—identifies exact enantiomorphic (chiral) congruence, the very relation tested when Euclid applies inversely oriented congruent triangles in *Elements* I.5 (Pons Asinorum) without altering metric equality.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae* (Chapter IV, § 2, fn. 9, citing *In II De Caelo*, lect. 2, n. 11 on how length precedes breadth because according to geometers a moving line generates a surface, and Chapter IV, § 4.2, pp. 183–205 on the notion of *direction* and orientation), Peter Hoenen S.J. develops Aquinas's distinction between intrinsic vital polarity and relational geometric position into a rigorous theory of spatial isotropy and relative orientation. Pure geometric extension (*materia intelligibilis*) is completely homogeneous and isotropic: no point or axis possesses an intrinsic *above* or *right* prior to a chosen reference line. Yet once a single directed line *a* passing through a point *P* in a plane is posited, two opposite senses of angular divergence ('on the right' and 'on the left' relative to *a*, p. 194) immediately become objectively distinguishable as relational *differences in site alone*. Thus Hoenen shows how Aquinas's *per comparationem ad nos* in *De Caelo* II.2 translates mathematically into frame-relative orientation and reflection symmetry, preserving Euclidean invariance across every rotation of the coordinate frame.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's demonstration in *In II De Caelo*, lect. 2 that geometric figures possess no absolute *up*, *down*, *left*, or *right* in themselves—acquiring directional labels solely relative to an adopted reference frame and inverting chirality under mirror reflection—captures a foundational principle of symbolic modeling in ``geometor.model`` and ``geometor.divine``. Although ``geometor.model`` typically seeds a canonical construction with two initial points along a horizontal axis at ``(0, 0)`` and ``(1, 0)`` to fix a reference orientation (*quoad nos*), the emergent golden sections, harmonic ranges, and equilateral or pentagonal symmetries detected by ``geometor.divine`` are completely invariant under rigid rotation, translation, and mirror reflection (*in speculo*). Moreover, Aquinas's observation in nn. 9 and 13 that right and left agree in *figure* (*conveniunt in figura*) while reversing orientation anticipates bilateral and chiral symmetry analysis in ``geometor.phyllotaxis`` and ``geometor.seer``, where parastichy spirals (clockwise versus counterclockwise Fibonacci numbers) and visual grid transformations exhibit exact mirror duality.
